source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Founding claim. Groups, like people, show one general factor across tasks. The authors call it c, by analogy with g.
numbers: Two studies, 699 people, groups of 2 to 5. Defined c as the general ability of a group to do many tasks.
quote: By analogy with individual intelligence, we define a group's collective intelligence (c) as the general ability of the group to perform a wide variety of tasks.
limits: c is an inference from correlations among task scores. It is a statistical factor, not a measured mechanism.
agent_relevance: Any c-like claim for agents is the same kind of inference: a positive manifold among task scores, nothing more.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Study 1 design and factor result. 40 three-person groups worked up to 5 hours on tasks from the McGrath circumplex plus a criterion task.
numbers: Study 1: 40 groups of 3. Mean inter-task correlation r=0.28. First factor eigenvalue accounted for over 43% of variance, second only 18%. One-factor CFA chi2=1.66, P=0.89, df=5.
limits: Only 40 groups. Few tasks (about 5 plus criterion). Tasks chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Small samples with few tasks give wobbly factor shares. Treat 43% as one noisy estimate.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Study 2 replicated Study 1 inside the same paper with a larger sample and different tasks.
numbers: Study 2: 152 groups of 2 to 5. First factor 44%, second 20%. CFA chi2=5.85, P=0.32, df=5, CFI=0.98, RMSEA=0.03. A subset got 10 tasks. Parallel analysis kept one factor (eigenvalue cut 1.38). Multi-group CFA showed invariance across studies, chi2=11.34, df=14.
limits: Same lab, same authors, same task family. Not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: Shows the c structure was stable within one lab's task battery.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Individual intelligence did not predict c strongly. This made c look like a new group property.
numbers: Pooled across studies: mean member intelligence r=0.15 (P=0.04) with c, max member intelligence r=0.19 (P=0.008). Study 1 criterion task: c b=0.51 (P=0.001), mean IQ b=0.08, max IQ b=0.01 (ns). Study 2 criterion: c b=0.36 (P=0.0001), mean IQ b=0.05, max IQ b=0.12 (ns).
limits: Study 1 had only n=40 groups, so low power. Later work (Bates and Gupta) found a much stronger link.
agent_relevance: Key point: c beat average member ability in predicting a criterion task. Disputed later.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Correlates of c: social sensitivity, even turn-taking, share of women. Cohesion, motivation and satisfaction did not predict c.
numbers: Proportion female r=0.23 (P=0.007), mostly mediated by social sensitivity (Sobel z=1.93, P=0.03). Women scored higher on Reading the Mind in the Eyes (RME), t(441)=3.42.
limits: Correlational. The mediation test is weak. Sociometric badges used in Study 2.
agent_relevance: These social correlates do not transfer to LLM agents (no eyes, no turn-taking), so only the factor logic is portable.

source: Woolley et al. (2010) Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups
finding: Comparison with individual g. First factors in individual tests explain 30 to 50% of variance, so 43% was called typical.
numbers: Wonderlic scores of 642 individuals used as the comparison scree plot in Fig 2. Individual-test first factor 30 to 50%.
quote: the first factor extracted in a factor analysis of these scores generally accounts for 30 to 50% of the variance
limits: Factor share depends on the number and similarity of tasks. With 5 to 10 tasks, a share of variance is not comparable to a 100-item test.
agent_relevance: Variance share is a weak yardstick. Do not quote 43% as proof of general ability.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Large pooled test of c. 22 studies run on one platform (POGS), meta-analytic two-stage factor model.
numbers: 22 studies, 5,279 individuals, 1,356 groups, groups of 2 to 7. 8 task types, 4 to 8 per study. Three tasks in all studies (Brainstorm Object, Typing Text, Unscramble Words). Average inter-item correlation 0.27 (range 0.12 to 0.50). Loadings 0.27 to 0.52, all P<0.001.
quote: We find strong support for a general factor of CI using meta-analytic methods
limits: All 22 samples used the same platform and the same research group. Different tasks per study, so the pooled matrix is incomplete. Same lab as the original.
agent_relevance: Pooled evidence is real but not independent of the original authors.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: The original text reported average variance extracted (AVE) of 44%. This was later corrected to 19.6%.
numbers: Original: average variance extracted of 44%. Loading range 0.27 to 0.52. Original SI fit for the 8-task Model 4: chi2(28)=466.8, CFI 0.83, RMSEA 0.052.
limits: 44% echoed the headline number of Woolley 2010 and made it look like a clean replication. The corrected number is less than half.
agent_relevance: The honest strength of c across 22 studies is closer to one fifth than two fifths of task variance.

source: Correction for Riedl et al. (2022) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Official correction: AVE was wrong because of a software mistake.
numbers: Text changed from 44% to 19.6%. Loadings stayed 0.27 to 0.52 (Model 1: 0.35 to 0.50). Corrected SI Model 4 fit chi2(20, N=1,356)=93.284, CFI=0.833, RMSEA=0.052 [0.042-0.063]. Model 2 (5 tasks) chi2(5)=19.514, CFI=0.93, RMSEA=0.046. Authors say all models still support one factor.
quote: due to a mistake in a software package, the average variance extracted (AVE) for the factor analyses reported in SI Appendix, Table S4 are incorrect
limits: The authors call fit good, though CFI 0.83 for the 8-task model is under the usual 0.90 cut.
agent_relevance: Central number of the dispute. A sceptic reads 19.6% plus CFI 0.83 as weak. A defender reads positive loadings as enough.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Leave-one-out test: c computed from 7 tasks predicts the 8th.
numbers: Average Pearson r=0.40 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.53), all P<0.001. One SD higher CI went with about 18% (plus or minus 12%) better task performance.
limits: r=0.40 means about 16% of variance in the held-out task. Medium, not large, in practice.
agent_relevance: Cross-task prediction is the useful test of any general factor. It is modest here.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: What predicts c in the 22-study data. Process beats individual skill and composition.
numbers: Random forest: collaboration process (skill congruence, strategy, effort) most important, then individual skill (mean, max), then group size, social perceptiveness, composition (proportion female, age diversity). For Sudoku over 51% of explained variation was individual skill. For Unscramble Words, 55% was group process.
limits: Importance varies by task. Authors say split findings in the literature come from task choice and from rules that limit who can enter the answer.
agent_relevance: Suggests c is partly a task-mix artifact, which is the sceptic's point.

source: Riedl et al. (2021) Quantifying collective intelligence in human groups
finding: Authors name the critics and offer their explanation of the failures to replicate.
numbers: They cite others who questioned the results (refs 22, 23) and disparate results on individual skill (ref 24). They blame differing task choice and constrained interaction rules.
limits: This is an explanation by the original lab. Not independently tested.
agent_relevance: The dispute is partly about measurement choices, not only about truth.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence
finding: Independent replication in Edinburgh and Chennai: a group factor appears, but it is mostly individual IQ.
numbers: Three studies, 312 people. Study 1: 72 people, 26 groups of 2 to 4; parallel analysis one factor, 39.8% of variance, eigenvalues 1.98, 0.85, 0.69, 0.69, 0.79. Study 2: 120 people in India. Study 3: 40 groups of 3 in Edinburgh. Group factor about 50% of variance in Study 2.
quote: individual IQ accounted for around 80% of group-IQ differences
limits: Small samples (Study 1 had 58% power for the r=0.36 social-sensitivity effect). Raven used for both individual IQ and a group task in Study 1. Reviewers questioned raffle motivation in India.
agent_relevance: A general factor of group scores does replicate. What fails is the claim that it is separate from member ability.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence
finding: Regression: only individual IQ predicted the group factor.
numbers: Study 1 model R2=57%: individual IQ beta=0.76 [0.4,1.12], t=4.37, p<0.001. Proportion female beta=0.12 (p=0.447). RME beta=-0.11 (p=0.520). Group size beta=0.28 (p=0.075).
limits: Study 2 alone showed an RME link to group-IQ scores. Authors dismiss it in the joint model.
agent_relevance: Gender and empathy effects did not replicate in these three samples.

source: Bates and Gupta (2017) Smart groups of smart people: evidence for IQ as the origin of collective intelligence
finding: Structural model across Studies 2 and 3 (best model D): RME has no effect on the latent group factor.
numbers: Model A (RME only) fit poorly: chi2(537)=105.65, CFI=0.601, RMSEA=0.312. Best model: IQ drives group-IQ, RME touches only one task (missing letters). Overlap of group-IQ and average individual IQ called indistinguishable from 100%.
quote: Smart groups are (simply) groups of smart people.
limits: Authors say group tests would be redundant given individual IQ tests. Woolley's side replied that an unmeasured moderator must exist.
agent_relevance: A group factor can just be the average ability of members. For our agent: c of a multi-agent set-up may just be base-model strength.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? ToM predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face
finding: Same-lab extension: c also appears in online text-only groups with a new task battery.
numbers: 68 groups (power analysis: 60 needed), randomly assigned face-to-face or online. First factor explained 49% (face-to-face) and 41% (online) of variance, second factor under half of that.
limits: Same research group, new battery. Does not address the critique about effort and nesting.
agent_relevance: Evidence for c in text-only teams, which resemble LLM chat groups more than face-to-face groups do.

source: Engel, Woolley, Jing, Chabris, Malone (2014) Reading the Mind in the Eyes or reading between the lines? ToM predicts collective intelligence equally well online and face-to-face
finding: Theory of mind (RME) predicts c equally in both modes. Women share also predicts.
numbers: RME with c: r=.53 (p=.002) face-to-face, r=.55 (p<.001) online. Proportion women with c r=.41 (p=.01) online. More total communication went with higher c, uneven contribution with lower c. Two low-RME outliers removed: r=.47 and .48.
limits: Mediation of gender by RME again. Group-level N small (about 34 per condition).
agent_relevance: Social-skill claims survive in this lab and fail in Bates and Gupta. The split is itself informative.

source: Barlow and Dennis (2016) Not as smart as we think: a study of collective intelligence in virtual groups (summary via LSE Business Review blog)
finding: Failed replication in text-chat groups: no c factor.
numbers: 324 participants, 86 groups of 3 to 5, Gmail chat, four tasks (brainstorm, decision, negotiation, combined). Average inter-task correlation -0.05. No single factor for all four tasks or for any set of three or more. Pilot: 91 individuals, individual factor correlated r=0.318 with an IQ test.
limits: Read from a blog summary, not the paper (paywalled). Loadings only in figures. Opposes Engel 2014, which also used online groups but a different battery.
agent_relevance: Different task batteries give opposite answers on c in online groups. c depends on the battery.

source: Credé and Howardson (2017) The structure of group task performance: a second look at collective intelligence. Comment on Woolley et al. (2010), J Applied Psychology 102(10), 1483-1492 (press summary)
finding: Reanalysis of six published samples argues the evidence for c is weak.
numbers: Six studies reanalysed. Only one (a 2014 Indiana University study) concluded no evidence of c. Press says low effort and nested data may inflate small cross-task correlations.
limits: Read from a university press release, not the paper (paywalled). The press piece gives no sample sizes or statistics.
agent_relevance: Gives two testable mechanisms: low effort and nesting. Both apply to agents (lazy or degenerate outputs).

source: Credé and Howardson (2017) critique, press detail on mechanisms
finding: Credé's arguments in plain words: unmotivated participants, near-zero scores, averaged individual responses.
numbers: Example: brainstorming bricks task, 10 minutes, one point per use; at least one team scored zero. Participants were students for course credit or paid community members. Woolley team found equal speaking turns went with better performance.
limits: Press paraphrase only. Credé grants that performance on one task may predict a similar task.
agent_relevance: Low-effort floor effects create a positive manifold. Check for zero scores and floor effects before trusting any c.

source: Woolley, Kim, Malone (2018) Measuring collective intelligence in groups: a reply to Credé and Howardson, MIT Sloan Research Paper 5431-18
finding: The authors' reply exists. Only bibliographic metadata was readable.
numbers: Metadata only: MIT Sloan Research Paper No. 5431-18, June 2018. A web search summary says it disputes the effort and ability artifact claims.
limits: Abstract and arguments NOT read (SSRN returned 403, lab page lists metadata only).
agent_relevance: Do not cite the reply's content from this entry.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: First direct test of a c-like factor in LLM agent groups. They find one: an Artificial Collective Intelligence (ACI) factor.
numbers: 108 LLM groups: sizes 3, 5, 8; rounds 2 or 3; topologies decentralized, centralized, random; homogeneous or mixed LLMs. Eight LLMs (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4o-mini, Qwen2.5 7B/32B/72B, GLM-4-9B, InternLM2.5-20B, Gemma-2-27B). 5 tasks: commonsense, math, games, coding, writing. Average inter-task r=0.55. First factor 66.3% of variance, second 18.7%. Human figure quoted as 43%.
quote: an ACI factor can be extracted from LLM agent groups to predict the generalization performance on new tasks
limits: Only 5 tasks and 108 groups. Groups vary in base-model quality (single-model scores 0.40 to 0.81 across tasks), which alone can create a positive manifold. One framework (multi-agent debate). Authors admit it is empirical, no theory.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant. A larger shared factor than in humans (66% vs about 20 to 44%) is a red flag for model strength rather than a group property. Do not lean on ACI for design.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Leave-one-out test: ACI from 4 tasks predicts the 5th.
numbers: Correlations above 0.8 on three tasks and about 0.5 on the rest, all significant. Random forest from group features predicts ACI with R2 above 0.8 and most task scores with R2 above 0.6.
limits: Model-strength confound not separated from group structure.
agent_relevance: High predictability may reflect simple things such as which LLM sits in the group.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: What drives ACI in LLM groups: who sits where, not size or rounds.
numbers: Random forest importance: skill congruence over 50%, mean individual intelligence 37%, max individual intelligence, group size and effort each under 5%. Fully connected network was not better than centralized with a strong agent at the hub. One group cost 75% more but its ACI was only 9.7% higher than the cheaper group.
limits: Mirrors the Riedl 2021 importance pattern, which may be by construction (same indicator design).
agent_relevance: Putting the strongest model at the high-degree node beats adding agents or rounds.

source: Zhou et al. (2026) Identifying Collective Intelligence Factor in LLM Agent Groups for Generalizable Multi-Agent System Design
finding: Using predicted ACI as an extra objective in two multi-agent design methods improved unseen-task scores.
numbers: Plug-in to GPTSwarm and G-Designer: gains 1.1% to 12.3% on unseen tasks, average 4.6%.
limits: Small gains. No seed variance shown in the text. Compared with task-specific optimisation, not with a best single model.
agent_relevance: Modest practical value. It does not show that a c exists beyond model strength.

source: Riedl (2025) Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models
finding: Different approach: tests whether LLM groups are real collectives with information theory, not a c factor.
numbers: Group guessing game with GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1 8B and 70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3. Three prompt conditions: plain, persona, persona plus think-about-what-others-might-do. Plain groups: strong temporal synergy, little coordinated alignment. Persona: identity-linked differentiation. Persona plus ToM prompt: goal-directed complementarity.
quote: Without attributing human-like cognition to the agents, the patterns of interaction we observe mirror well-established principles of collective intelligence
limits: No c factor computed. Simple guessing task. Result is about prompts steering coordination.
agent_relevance: A cheap lever: a theory-of-mind prompt changes group structure. Neither supports nor refutes c.
